title: Gloves between tasks
stem: After perineal care, the nurse must clean the same client's mouth. What should occur before oral care?
options: Continue with the gloves used for perineal care
Remove gloves, clean hands and put on fresh gloves
Disinfect the used gloves with hand rub
Remove used gloves and put on a fresh pair
why: The used gloves may transfer enteric organisms to the mouth.
Both glove change and hand hygiene interrupt dirty-to-clean transfer.
Hand rub does not make disposable gloves suitable for reuse.
A new pair does not remove organisms transferred to hands during removal.
takeaway: Change gloves and clean hands between contaminated and clean tasks.
learningObjective: Change gloves and clean hands between contaminated and clean tasks.

title: Visible soil
stem: A nurse's hands are visibly soiled after removing gloves. What is appropriate?
options: Apply alcohol rub over the soil
Use a disinfectant surface wipe
Wash with soap and water
Put on clean gloves first
why: Visible soil requires physical removal rather than alcohol rub alone.
Surface products may damage skin and are not hand cleansers.
Soap and water remove visible contamination.
New gloves do not remove contamination already on hands.
takeaway: Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
learningObjective: Use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.

title: Patient-zone contact
stem: A nurse adjusts a client's bedside table without touching the client, then prepares another client's medication. What is required?
options: Clean hands only after medication preparation
Use gloves during medication preparation
Treat table contact as clean
Perform hand hygiene before moving to the next task
why: Contamination should not enter the medication preparation area.
Gloves cannot replace hand hygiene after environmental contact.
Patient surroundings can carry transmissible organisms.
Hand hygiene interrupts transfer from the patient environment.
takeaway: Patient surroundings can contaminate hands without direct client contact.
learningObjective: Patient surroundings can contaminate hands without direct client contact.

title: Wet alcohol rub
stem: After the nurse applies alcohol hand rub, the hands remain wet. What is appropriate before putting on gloves?
options: Continue rubbing until the hands are dry
Dry the hands with a clean paper towel
Put gloves on while the product remains wet
Rinse the product off with clean water
why: Rubbing through drying completes the intended application.
Premature wiping removes product before its application is complete.
Gloves over wet product can impair use and irritate skin.
Rinsing interrupts the intended hand-rub process.
takeaway: Allow hand rub to dry before putting on gloves.
learningObjective: Allow hand rub to dry before putting on gloves.

title: Hand skin damage
stem: A nurse develops cracked, painful hand skin during a period of frequent hand hygiene. What is the best response?
options: Switch every encounter to soap and water
Seek skin assessment and compatible product guidance
Wear two glove layers for every client encounter
Apply a personal moisturizer before each glove change
why: More soap-and-water exposure may worsen irritation and does not identify the cause.
Assessment and compatible products support skin recovery while maintaining hygiene.
Additional gloves do not treat damaged skin or replace hand hygiene.
Personal products may be incompatible with gloves or workplace antiseptics.
takeaway: Address skin damage while maintaining effective hand hygiene.
learningObjective: Address skin damage while maintaining effective hand hygiene.

title: Glove tear
stem: A glove tears while the nurse handles soiled linen; no skin injury occurs. What next?
options: Finish all room tasks first
Cover the tear with another glove
Remove gloves, clean hands and replace as needed
Use alcohol rub on the torn glove
why: The barrier breach requires prompt hand hygiene.
Covering the tear does not remove possible hand contamination.
This restores hand cleanliness and the needed barrier.
Glove disinfection does not address contamination beneath the tear.
takeaway: Respond to a glove breach by cleaning hands and replacing barriers.
learningObjective: Respond to a glove breach by cleaning hands and replacing barriers.

title: Mask front contact
stem: During mask removal, the nurse touches its used front with bare fingers and is about to use a shared charting tablet. What should happen?
options: Chart first and then disinfect the tablet
Put gloves on before handling the tablet
Complete documentation and then wash hands
Clean hands before touching the tablet
why: Cleaning later allows avoidable contamination of the device during use.
Gloves over potentially contaminated hands do not resolve the hand-hygiene need.
Delayed hand hygiene permits transfer to a shared surface.
The mask front may contaminate fingers, requiring cleaning before clean contact.
takeaway: Correct removal errors with prompt hand hygiene.
learningObjective: Correct removal errors with prompt hand hygiene.

title: PPE preparation
stem: A nurse will empty liquid stool and clean an incontinent client; splashing toward the face is anticipated. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Select gloves and clothing protection for the exposure
Arrange mask and eye protection for anticipated splashes
Treat a procedure mask as protection for both mouth and eyes
Use ordinary prescription glasses for eye protection
Plan safe barrier removal and hand hygiene
why: Contact with stool and clothing contamination are foreseeable.
Eye and mucous-membrane exposure need appropriate facial protection.
A mask does not protect the eyes from splashes.
Ordinary glasses do not provide the splash coverage of appropriate protective eyewear.
Safe removal limits self-contamination after the task.
takeaway: Combine posted precautions with a task-specific exposure assessment.
learningObjective: Combine posted precautions with a task-specific exposure assessment.

title: Respirator seal
stem: Before entering an airborne-precaution room, a fit-tested nurse cannot obtain a seal with the assigned respirator. What next?
options: Enter briefly without adjusting it
Obtain suitable respiratory protection before entry
Tighten the surgical mask over it
Rely on the previous fit test
why: A brief exposure can still occur through a poor seal.
Effective protection requires an appropriate device and seal.
Layering a mask does not establish respirator fit.
Fit testing does not replace a seal check at each use.
takeaway: Do not enter an airborne-risk area with an inadequate respirator seal.
learningObjective: Do not enter an airborne-risk area with an inadequate respirator seal.

title: Respirator versus mask
stem: A transport worker plans to enter a suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis room wearing a procedure mask. What should the nurse do?
options: Permit entry once the client puts on a procedure mask
Add a face shield to the worker's procedure mask
Arrange the required respirator and safe-use instruction
Ask the worker to remain inside only briefly
why: Client source control does not replace required worker protection during entry.
A face shield does not convert a procedure mask into a respirator.
The worker needs protection suited to the airborne exposure.
A brief entry can still create airborne exposure.
takeaway: Match worker respiratory protection to the exposure route.
learningObjective: Match worker respiratory protection to the exposure route.

title: TB transport
stem: A client with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis needs essential imaging. Which transport plan best reduces exposure?
options: Send now and inform imaging when the client arrives
Notify imaging but leave client masking until arrival
Mask the client and use the usual waiting-area queue
Coordinate imaging and route; mask the client if tolerated
why: Late notification prevents the receiving service from preparing.
Source control is needed during transport when tolerated.
A shared waiting queue can expose others unnecessarily.
Advance coordination and client source control reduce transit and waiting exposure.
takeaway: Coordinate source control and receiving-area precautions during transport.
learningObjective: Coordinate source control and receiving-area precautions during transport.

title: Measles waiting area
stem: A child with fever, cough and a new rash has a known measles exposure. What is the priority in a crowded clinic?
options: Separate promptly using the airborne-risk pathway
Wait for laboratory confirmation before placement
Seat beside other coughing children
Complete registration before precautions
why: Compatible symptoms and exposure justify immediate containment measures.
Waiting can expose susceptible people before confirmation.
Similar symptoms do not establish the same infection.
Administrative tasks should not delay exposure reduction.
takeaway: Begin indicated precautions from clinical suspicion, not only confirmed tests.
learningObjective: Begin indicated precautions from clinical suspicion, not only confirmed tests.

title: Disseminated zoster
stem: An immunocompromised client has widespread suspected zoster lesions. Which precaution plan should the nurse verify?
options: Contact precautions alone
Airborne and contact precautions
Droplet precautions alone
Routine practices only after covering one lesion
why: Widespread zoster also presents airborne transmission concerns.
Combined precautions address airborne and lesion-contact exposure.
Droplet precautions do not adequately address the indicated routes.
Covering one lesion cannot contain widespread disease.
takeaway: Disseminated zoster requires combined route-specific precautions.
learningObjective: Disseminated zoster requires combined route-specific precautions.

title: Uncontained drainage
stem: A purulent wound dressing repeatedly leaks onto bedding. What is the best initial infection-control plan?
options: Obtain the culture result before selecting precautions
Replace the dressing on the usual schedule
Contain drainage and institute indicated contact measures
Monitor temperature to determine when precautions are needed
why: Clinical contamination risk exists while the organism is being identified.
The usual schedule is inadequate when drainage repeatedly escapes.
Containment and route-specific precautions address current environmental spread.
Fever does not determine whether leaking drainage can transmit organisms.
takeaway: Uncontained secretions can require additional contact precautions.
learningObjective: Uncontained secretions can require additional contact precautions.

title: New diarrhoea cluster
stem: Three residents develop vomiting and diarrhoea over one shift. What should the nurse do first?
options: Wait for every stool culture
Continue communal meals pending a diagnosis
Compare menus before changing care
Notify the outbreak/IPAC lead and institute indicated precautions
why: Waiting for confirmation can permit further transmission.
Group activities may spread an infectious syndrome.
Dietary review may help investigation but should not delay containment.
A cluster warrants prompt coordinated assessment and precautions.
takeaway: Recognize clusters early and initiate the outbreak response pathway.
learningObjective: Recognize clusters early and initiate the outbreak response pathway.

title: Suspected C. difficile
stem: A client develops frequent unformed stools after antibiotics. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Initiate the local enteric-precaution pathway
Use dedicated toileting equipment where feasible
Wait for confirmation before changing room practices
Promptly communicate the symptoms for assessment
why: The clinical presentation warrants early transmission precautions.
Dedicated equipment reduces indirect spread.
Delay may expose others while tests are pending.
Assessment is needed for causes, hydration and treatment planning.
takeaway: Act on suspected infectious diarrhoea while assessment proceeds.
learningObjective: Act on suspected infectious diarrhoea while assessment proceeds.

title: Precaution discontinuation
stem: A client colonized with a resistant organism has no symptoms and asks to stop precautions. What should guide the decision?
options: The absence of current wound drainage
The local organism-specific discontinuation criteria
Completion of the latest antibiotic course
A negative screening result from a previous admission
why: Lack of drainage does not necessarily establish absence of carriage.
Discontinuation depends on the organism, setting and current criteria.
Treatment completion does not automatically establish clearance.
A historical result may not represent current colonization.
takeaway: Use organism- and setting-specific criteria to stop precautions.
learningObjective: Use organism- and setting-specific criteria to stop precautions.

title: Isolation-related missed care
stem: A client on contact precautions understands the call bell but waits so long for toileting help that they have been incontinent twice. What plan best addresses the gap?
options: Repeat call-bell teaching at each medication round
Bring extra continence supplies for each shift
Schedule reliable toileting contacts using required precautions
Limit assistance to routine medication-round visits
why: The client already knows how to request help.
Supplies manage consequences but do not provide timely assistance.
Planned care directly addresses the delay while maintaining precautions.
Fixed medication rounds may not match toileting needs.
takeaway: Additional precautions must not reduce access to necessary care.
learningObjective: Additional precautions must not reduce access to necessary care.

title: Visitor PPE teaching
stem: A visitor can describe written PPE-removal steps but contaminates their hands while practising. What teaching method is most useful next?
options: Provide an additional illustrated instruction sheet
Repeat the removal steps aloud at a slower pace
Ask the visitor to recite the sequence once more
Demonstrate removal and observe a return demonstration
why: The identified gap is practical performance rather than access to written steps.
Verbal explanation alone may not correct the motor sequence.
The visitor already demonstrates recall of the steps.
Observed practice lets the nurse correct the actual contamination error.
takeaway: Evaluate PPE teaching through observed performance.
learningObjective: Evaluate PPE teaching through observed performance.

title: Shared room diarrhoea
stem: A newly incontinent client with suspected infectious diarrhoea shares a room with a highly vulnerable client. What should happen?
options: Request placement review and begin indicated precautions
Wait for a positive test before acting
Separate beds with a curtain only
Transfer the roommate's supplies but keep shared toileting
why: Contamination risk and roommate vulnerability require prompt placement review.
Clinical suspicion can justify action before confirmation.
A curtain does not address shared contact surfaces.
Shared toileting remains a major exposure route.
takeaway: Consider source containment and roommate vulnerability in placement.
learningObjective: Consider source containment and roommate vulnerability in placement.

title: Cohorting uncertainty
stem: Two clients have vomiting but no confirmed diagnosis. What should guide cohorting?
options: Cohort them because symptoms began on the same day
Use IPAC assessment of likely organisms and compatibility
Use the available double room
Use a shared room if both remain afebrile
why: Similar timing does not establish the same infection.
Assessment considers transmission and each client's vulnerability.
Availability alone does not establish safe placement.
Absence of fever does not confirm compatible pathogens.
takeaway: Do not assume matching symptoms establish safe cohorting.
learningObjective: Do not assume matching symptoms establish safe cohorting.

title: Respiratory source control
stem: A coughing client arrives in a crowded clinic for a nonurgent appointment. What should the nurse do first?
options: Complete the full clinical history
Seat the client in the main waiting area
Apply respiratory hygiene and separation measures
Arrange the next available same-day assessment slot
why: Initial exposure reduction should not await a complete history.
Crowded placement increases opportunities for transmission.
Early source control and separation protect others during assessment.
Booking clinical review matters, but immediate exposure measures come first.
takeaway: Apply respiratory source control at first presentation.
learningObjective: Apply respiratory source control at first presentation.

title: Aerosol procedure planning
stem: A stable client requires a nonemergency aerosol-generating diagnostic procedure. The equipped room and trained team will be available in two hours; the current room lacks the required controls. What is best?
options: Perform now using procedure masks and face shields
Perform now with fewer staff in the current room
Wait for a confirmed diagnosis before considering the procedure
Schedule the equipped room with required respiratory protection
why: Procedure masks do not replace the required aerosol-risk protection.
Reducing staff count does not correct inadequate controls.
The diagnostic procedure may be needed to establish the diagnosis.
The stable nonemergency context allows appropriate controls to be arranged safely.
takeaway: Resolve required aerosol-procedure controls before proceeding when feasible.
learningObjective: Resolve required aerosol-procedure controls before proceeding when feasible.

title: Exposure notification
stem: A staff member learns of an unprotected exposure to a communicable infection. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Report through occupational health promptly
Provide timing and nature of exposure
Wait for symptoms before seeking advice
Follow individualized work and follow-up instructions
why: Prompt assessment may enable time-sensitive prevention.
Exposure details guide risk evaluation.
Some interventions are useful before symptoms appear.
Work restrictions and monitoring depend on the specific exposure.
takeaway: Use occupational health assessment after unprotected exposure.
learningObjective: Use occupational health assessment after unprotected exposure.

title: Sick food handler
stem: A nurse with active vomiting is scheduled to help with resident meal service. What should occur?
options: Attend with gloves only
Notify the supervisor and follow illness-exclusion guidance
Work if no fever is present
Restrict work to preparing cold foods
why: Gloves alone do not control all enteric transmission risks.
Illness management protects residents and supports appropriate return-to-work decisions.
Vomiting illness can be infectious without fever.
Cold-food preparation can still contaminate ready-to-eat food.
takeaway: Report potentially infectious illness before direct care or food handling.
learningObjective: Report potentially infectious illness before direct care or food handling.

title: Laundry handling
stem: A linen sheet is heavily contaminated with stool. What handling best limits spread?
options: Shake it before bagging
Carry it against the uniform
Contain it at the point of use without shaking
Rinse it in the handwashing sink
why: Shaking can disperse contaminated material.
Uniform contact can spread organisms beyond the room.
Containment limits environmental and clothing contamination.
The handwashing sink should not become a soiled-linen processing area.
takeaway: Contain soiled linen without dispersing contamination.
learningObjective: Contain soiled linen without dispersing contamination.

title: Leaking waste bag
stem: A contaminated waste bag starts leaking before it reaches the unit exit. What should the nurse do first?
options: Transfer loose contents into a new bag by hand
Continue to the waste room and deal with the leak there
Clean the visible floor spill while leaving the bag leaking
Contain the leaking bag using the approved overpack process
why: Transferring contents adds avoidable handling and exposure.
Further transport may spread contamination along the route.
Cleanup will be undermined if the source remains uncontained.
Containing the source prevents continued leakage before safe removal and cleanup.
takeaway: Contain leaking contaminated material before transporting it.
learningObjective: Contain leaking contaminated material before transporting it.

title: Contact time
stem: A disinfectant label requires the surface to remain wet for a specified contact time. The surface dries early. What next?
options: Reapply as directed to achieve the required wet time
Assume wiping completed disinfection
Dry it further with a towel
Dilute the product to slow evaporation
why: Label-directed wet exposure is necessary for the claimed disinfection.
Wiping alone may not achieve the required microbial effect.
Early drying shortens the intended exposure.
Unapproved dilution changes effectiveness and safety.
takeaway: Meet the disinfectant's labelled concentration and contact time.
learningObjective: Meet the disinfectant's labelled concentration and contact time.

title: Visible soil on equipment
stem: A reusable device has visible organic material on it before disinfection. What should happen first?
options: Apply a second layer of disinfectant over the material
Clean it according to the device instructions
Rinse briefly with water and dry the visible surface
Repeat the disinfection cycle at the usual concentration
why: Organic material can shield organisms despite more disinfectant.
Cleaning removes soil that can impair subsequent disinfection.
A brief rinse may not remove adherent material adequately.
Repeating disinfection does not replace the required cleaning step.
takeaway: Cleaning precedes effective disinfection or sterilization.
learningObjective: Cleaning precedes effective disinfection or sterilization.

title: Cleaning cloth transfer
stem: A cleaner uses a cloth on a toilet and then prepares to wipe a bedside table with it. What is the best correction?
options: Use a visibly clean corner of the same cloth
Rinse the cloth in the used cleaning bucket
Use appropriate fresh materials for the bedside surface
Rewet the same cloth with additional disinfectant
why: A clean-looking area does not establish absence of transferred organisms.
The used bucket may recontaminate the cloth.
Fresh materials avoid carrying heavy toilet contamination to a cleaner surface.
More product does not reliably correct inappropriate cloth reuse.
takeaway: Prevent dirty-to-clean transfer during environmental cleaning.
learningObjective: Prevent dirty-to-clean transfer during environmental cleaning.

title: Dilution uncertainty
stem: A fresh disinfectant batch is urgently needed. An unlabelled bottle sits beside the mixing station; an identified approved product and its instructions are available. What is safest?
options: Use the unlabelled bottle because it is beside the station
Ask the previous shift which dilution they usually prepare
Add fresh concentrate to the unlabelled contents
Use the verified product and prepare it as instructed
why: Location does not establish identity or correct concentration.
The usual recipe does not establish the identity or actual concentration of this unlabelled bottle.
Mixing unknown contents may create an unsafe concentration or reaction.
The available identified product permits an effective, reproducible preparation.
takeaway: Do not use an unidentified or unverified cleaning preparation.
learningObjective: Do not use an unidentified or unverified cleaning preparation.

title: Dedicated commode
stem: A dedicated commode is visibly soiled after use by a client with infectious diarrhoea. Emptying is likely to splash. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Clean and disinfect it according to the enteric-care protocol
Use protective barriers matched to the splash exposure
Omit cleaning because the same client will use it again
Share it with another diarrhoeal client between cleaning cycles
Remove barriers safely and perform hand hygiene afterward
why: Dedicated equipment still accumulates contamination and requires processing.
Emptying exposes clothing and mucous membranes as well as hands.
Dedication reduces sharing but does not eliminate environmental contamination.
Similar symptoms do not justify sharing contaminated equipment.
Removal and hand hygiene prevent spread after handling waste.
takeaway: Dedicated equipment complements rather than replaces routine precautions.
learningObjective: Dedicated equipment complements rather than replaces routine precautions.

title: Single-use device
stem: An unopened device package states 'single use.' A colleague proposes reusing it after a quick wipe. What should the nurse do?
options: Reuse if it looks intact
Follow the approved single-use and disposal instructions
Soak it in hand rub
Reserve it for another client with the same diagnosis
why: Visual integrity does not establish reprocessing suitability.
Labelled use and authorized processing determine safe reuse decisions.
Hand rub is not a validated device reprocessing method.
Matching diagnoses does not prevent cross-infection.
takeaway: Do not improvise reprocessing for single-use devices.
learningObjective: Do not improvise reprocessing for single-use devices.

title: Sterile package moisture
stem: A sterile dressing package is damp although unopened. What should the nurse do?
options: Dry the outside and use it
Open it beside the client to inspect
Replace the compromised package
Use it only on a small wound
why: Drying does not restore a compromised sterile barrier.
Visual inspection cannot establish retained sterility.
Moisture may compromise the package's protective barrier.
Wound size does not make compromised sterility acceptable.
takeaway: Reject sterile supplies with compromised packaging.
learningObjective: Reject sterile supplies with compromised packaging.

title: Sterile field unseen
stem: A sterile setup is left unattended outside the nurse's view. What is the safest interpretation?
options: It remains sterile if no one reports touching it
Only the outer edge needs replacement
A new sterile drape restores certainty
Sterility cannot be assured; establish a new setup
why: Absence of a reported touch does not verify the field.
An unobserved breach may involve the centre too.
A drape does not reliably undo unknown contamination.
A fresh setup restores a verifiable sterile process.
takeaway: Maintain observation of a sterile field throughout use.
learningObjective: Maintain observation of a sterile field throughout use.

title: Reaching across field
stem: A nurse needs an item beyond a sterile field. What is the best action?
options: Reposition supplies or obtain assistance
Reach quickly across the field
Cover the nonsterile sleeve with a clean towel
Ask the client to pass the item across
why: A different access route avoids bringing nonsterile clothing over the field.
Speed does not prevent contamination from the sleeve.
A clean towel is not necessarily a sterile barrier.
The client's hand and passed item may contaminate the field.
takeaway: Arrange supplies to avoid reaching nonsterile items over sterile areas.
learningObjective: Arrange supplies to avoid reaching nonsterile items over sterile areas.

title: Sterile glove boundary
stem: A sterile glove touches the bed rail before catheter insertion. What next?
options: Continue if the rail was recently cleaned
Replace the contaminated glove using aseptic technique
Apply alcohol rub to the glove
Use that hand only to hold the catheter
why: A cleaned rail is not a sterile surface.
Replacing the glove restores the required sterile barrier.
Hand rub does not re-sterilize the glove.
Holding the catheter would transfer contamination to an invasive device.
takeaway: Replace a sterile glove after contact with a nonsterile surface.
learningObjective: Replace a sterile glove after contact with a nonsterile surface.

title: Catheter system break
stem: A urinary catheter separates from its drainage tubing and the exposed connection is contaminated. What should the nurse arrange under the replacement protocol?
options: Reconnect the exposed original components
Wipe the exterior and reconnect the tubing
Aseptic replacement of the catheter and collecting system
Replace the bag and reconnect the original catheter
why: Reconnection can introduce organisms into the urinary tract.
External wiping does not restore internal sterility.
A contaminated system break requires the guideline-based sterile correction.
Changing only the bag leaves the compromised catheter connection in use.
takeaway: Treat a urinary drainage-system break as a contamination event.
learningObjective: Treat a urinary drainage-system break as a contamination event.

title: Drainage bag position
stem: A urinary drainage bag is resting on the floor and raised above bladder level during transfer. What should be corrected?
options: Correct the floor contact but leave the bag raised for the transfer
Empty the bag and keep it above the bladder to avoid dragging
Clamp the catheter throughout the transfer to prevent backflow
Keep it off the floor and below bladder level
why: Both external contamination and backflow risk need correction.
Emptying does not make an elevated drainage system appropriate.
Routine clamping is not the appropriate substitute for safe bag positioning.
Both environmental contamination and drainage direction require correction.
takeaway: Protect a urinary drainage bag from floor contact and backflow.
learningObjective: Protect a urinary drainage bag from floor contact and backflow.

title: Urinary catheter prevention
stem: A client's catheter was inserted for a short procedure that is now complete. Which actions reduce infection risk? Select all that apply.
options: Review whether the indication remains
Maintain a closed drainage system
Disconnect routinely for easier movement
Remove when authorized and no longer needed
why: Ongoing need should be reassessed rather than assumed.
A closed system limits organism entry.
Routine disconnection creates avoidable contamination opportunities.
Reducing unnecessary catheter duration reduces exposure risk.
takeaway: Review device necessity and preserve closed drainage.
learningObjective: Review device necessity and preserve closed drainage.

title: Specimen from catheter
stem: A culture is prescribed for a catheterized client's urine. Which method is appropriate?
options: Withdraw urine from the drainage bag
Disinfect the designated sampling port and sample as instructed
Disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing
Puncture nondesignated tubing to withdraw urine
why: Bag urine may be old or contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
The designated port allows aseptic collection while preserving the closed system.
Disconnection creates avoidable contamination risk.
Puncturing an undesigned site can damage the system and introduce organisms.
takeaway: Collect catheter specimens aseptically through the designated port.
learningObjective: Collect catheter specimens aseptically through the designated port.

title: Injection preparation area
stem: A nurse prepares injections beside a sink used for dirty equipment. What should change?
options: Use more frequent wiping only
Prepare fewer syringes at once
Move preparation to a designated clean area
Cover the sink drain during preparation
why: Wiping alone does not separate clean preparation from contamination sources.
Smaller batches do not resolve the unsuitable location.
A clean area protects medications and sterile supplies.
A drain cover does not control all nearby splash contamination.
takeaway: Separate clean medication preparation from contaminated processing areas.
learningObjective: Separate clean medication preparation from contaminated processing areas.

title: Multidose vial entry
stem: A nurse must enter a multidose vial again to prepare a new dose. What is required?
options: Reuse the prior syringe for the same client
Change only the needle on the prior syringe
Enter another area of the stopper
Disinfect the stopper and use new sterile equipment
why: A used syringe can contaminate vial contents even for the same client.
Needle replacement does not make a used syringe sterile.
An apparently untouched stopper area does not replace antisepsis.
Every entry needs appropriate stopper disinfection and a new sterile needle and syringe.
takeaway: Use new sterile equipment for every vial entry.
learningObjective: Use new sterile equipment for every vial entry.

title: Injection safety breach
stem: A used syringe accidentally re-enters a shared medication vial. What should the nurse do?
options: Remove the vial from use and report the breach
Reserve the vial for the client whose syringe entered it
Disinfect the stopper and resume shared use
Use a filter needle for subsequent doses
why: The contents may be contaminated and the exposure needs assessment.
Patient dedication after contamination does not authorize salvaging the compromised vial.
Surface cleaning cannot sterilize the contents.
A filter needle does not reliably remove infectious contamination.
takeaway: Quarantine a potentially contaminated shared medication vial.
learningObjective: Quarantine a potentially contaminated shared medication vial.

title: Sharps container capacity
stem: A sharps container has reached its marked fill line during a busy medication round. What next?
options: Push contents down with forceps
Close and replace it through the approved process
Leave new sharps on the cart temporarily
Continue until the lid cannot close
why: Manipulating contents increases puncture and exposure risk.
Timely replacement preserves safe point-of-use disposal.
Loose sharps create injury risk for others.
Overfilling compromises safe closure and disposal.
takeaway: Replace sharps containers at the indicated fill limit.
learningObjective: Replace sharps containers at the indicated fill limit.

title: Unexpected sharp in linen
stem: A nurse sees a used needle in a linen pile. What is the safest action?
options: Shake the linen into the hamper
Pick it up by hand through thick gloves
Secure the area and use the approved sharps retrieval method
Ask laundry staff to find it later
why: Shaking can hide or propel the sharp.
Gloves do not reliably prevent puncture.
Controlled retrieval avoids blind handling and exposure.
Deferring the hazard transfers risk to other workers.
takeaway: Do not blindly handle linen containing an exposed sharp.
learningObjective: Do not blindly handle linen containing an exposed sharp.

title: Blood splash to eye
stem: Blood splashes into a nurse's eye. Which action should begin first while help is arranged?
options: Notify the supervisor of the exposure
Telephone occupational health for assessment
Arrange assessment of the source exposure
Irrigate the eye promptly using the exposure protocol
why: Reporting is needed but should not delay immediate decontamination.
Occupational follow-up is time-sensitive after the immediate rinse begins.
Source assessment does not remove blood already contacting the eye.
Prompt irrigation reduces ongoing mucous-membrane contact.
takeaway: Irrigate exposed mucous membranes and seek prompt exposure assessment.
learningObjective: Irrigate exposed mucous membranes and seek prompt exposure assessment.

title: Sharps disposal setup
stem: A nurse prepares a bedside injection where no sharps container is within reach. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Arrange safe point-of-use disposal before starting
Keep the disposal route unobstructed
Plan to recap before walking to the utility room
Use the approved container rather than an improvised cup
why: Preparation avoids handling an exposed sharp unnecessarily.
An accessible route supports immediate disposal.
Recapping introduces avoidable needlestick risk.
Approved containers provide puncture-resistant containment.
takeaway: Plan sharps disposal before beginning the procedure.
learningObjective: Plan sharps disposal before beginning the procedure.

title: Specimen transport leak
stem: A blood specimen tube leaks inside its transport bag before dispatch. What is best?
options: Send it promptly before further leakage occurs
Contain it and obtain laboratory guidance about recollection and transport
Wipe the paperwork and send the original tube
Put the leaking tube in a new specimen bag and send it
why: Rapid dispatch does not establish safe or valid processing.
Containment and laboratory review address exposure and specimen suitability.
Clean paperwork does not fix the leaking container or sample integrity.
Overbagging may contain leakage but does not establish an acceptable specimen for analysis.
takeaway: Contain compromised specimens and verify safe laboratory handling.
learningObjective: Contain compromised specimens and verify safe laboratory handling.

title: Clean supply contamination
stem: A nurse places unused dressings from a contact-precaution room back on the shared clean cart. What should be reviewed?
options: Restock any unopened package because its sterile inner barrier is intact
Restock supplies if the client did not touch them directly
Room-exposed supply handling under local IPAC policy
Wipe every paper package with disinfectant before restocking
why: Outer packaging may contaminate the shared clean storage area.
Room exposure can contaminate packaging without direct client contact.
Local handling rules account for contamination of outer packaging.
An unvalidated wipe process may damage packaging and does not establish suitability for return.
takeaway: Protect shared clean supplies from patient-room contamination.
learningObjective: Protect shared clean supplies from patient-room contamination.

title: Fall despite low score
stem: A client scored low risk at admission but is now sedated after a procedure. What should guide mobility assistance?
options: The original score until tomorrow
The current sedation and functional assessment
The client's usual independence alone
Whether a fall has already occurred
why: Admission scoring may no longer reflect present function.
A new impairment requires updated precautions.
Baseline independence does not establish post-sedation safety.
Prevention should begin before an injury occurs.
takeaway: Reassess fall risk after a clinical or medication change.
learningObjective: Reassess fall risk after a clinical or medication change.

title: Unwitnessed fall
stem: A nurse finds a client on the floor reporting hip pain. What should happen before moving them routinely?
options: Obtain the incident form
Ask them to walk to test strength
Assess injury and summon appropriate help
Transfer immediately to preserve dignity
why: Documentation follows immediate assessment and care.
Weight bearing may worsen an unrecognized injury.
Assessment determines a safe response and transfer method.
Dignity matters, but unassessed movement can cause harm.
takeaway: Assess for injury before routine movement after a fall.
learningObjective: Assess for injury before routine movement after a fall.

title: Fall without pain
stem: An anticoagulated client has an unwitnessed fall and cannot recall whether their head struck the floor. They deny pain and ask to return to bed. Which action takes priority?
options: Assist the client back to bed using the usual transfer aid
Review medications that may have contributed to the fall
Schedule routine observations at the next regular interval
Assess for injury and activate the post-fall escalation protocol
why: Movement should follow an injury assessment and a safe transfer decision.
Medication review helps prevent recurrence but does not address possible current bleeding.
Uncertain head impact and anticoagulation require prompt assessment rather than routine timing.
An unwitnessed fall with possible head impact can cause occult bleeding despite absent pain.
takeaway: Absence of pain does not exclude serious post-fall injury.
learningObjective: Absence of pain does not exclude serious post-fall injury.

title: Alarm as sole precaution
stem: A confused client repeatedly tries to stand despite a working bed alarm. During each attempt, they pull at their trousers and say they need to go home. What should the nurse do next?
options: Assess toileting needs, discomfort and reasons for getting up
Move the bed closer to the nursing station
Increase the sensitivity of the bed alarm
Repeat teaching about using the call bell
why: The behaviour may communicate an unmet need; identifying it guides timely assistance.
Proximity may help observation but does not identify why this client keeps rising.
The functioning alarm is already detecting movement; sensitivity does not address its cause.
Confusion may limit retention, and repeated teaching may miss the immediate need.
takeaway: Alarms supplement individualized fall prevention.
learningObjective: Alarms supplement individualized fall prevention.

title: Footwear mismatch
stem: A client walks safely with a prescribed aid but their open-back slippers slide off during turns. Which footwear should the nurse recommend?
options: Soft open-back slippers with a cushioned lining
Well-fitting shoes with secure closures and nonslip soles
Roomy slip-on shoes that accommodate thick socks
Firm-soled shoes with smooth leather soles
why: Cushioning does not prevent an unsecured heel from slipping out.
A secure fit and traction address the observed loss of footwear during turns.
An overly roomy slip-on fit may still allow heel movement during walking.
A firm sole may provide support, but a smooth sole offers less traction.
takeaway: Match fall prevention to the specific observed hazard.
learningObjective: Match fall prevention to the specific observed hazard.

title: Post-fall review
stem: A client fell while reaching across the bed for a hearing aid. Injury assessment is complete and strength is unchanged from admission. Which actions help prevent recurrence? Select all that apply.
options: Review placement of frequently used items
Explore how the client requests assistance
Retain the admission plan based on unchanged strength
Revise the mobility plan with the client
why: The reaching mechanism identifies an environmental hazard that can be corrected.
A communication or access barrier may explain why help was not obtained.
Unchanged strength does not eliminate the newly identified reaching hazard.
The plan should respond to the actual circumstances and the client's priorities.
takeaway: Use the event sequence to guide post-fall prevention.
learningObjective: Use the event sequence to guide post-fall prevention.

title: New visual deficit
stem: Following assessment of a new visual field deficit, a medically stable client repeatedly strikes doorframes with a walker. A move to independent hallway walking is planned this morning. What should the nurse do first?
options: Teach scanning during the planned independent walk
Move hallway obstacles before starting independent walking
Reassess mobility with rehabilitation support before progression
Limit walking to the familiar route used yesterday
why: Scanning may be useful, but it needs supervised assessment before independent progression.
Environmental clearance cannot fully address difficulty detecting fixed doorframes.
Repeated collisions show the present plan does not match function; supervised reassessment can establish safe assistance and adaptations.
Familiarity does not establish safety after a new field deficit.
takeaway: Reassess safe mobility after sensory or neurological change.
learningObjective: Reassess safe mobility after sensory or neurological change.

title: Unsafe bathroom urgency
stem: A client receiving a morning diuretic needs one-person assistance to walk. They correctly demonstrate call-bell use but have twice started walking while waiting during the expected period of urinary urgency. Which change best addresses this pattern?
options: Review the fall-prevention instructions at each shift
Ask the prescriber to review the medication schedule
Place a written reminder beside the call bell
Schedule assisted toileting before and during peak urgency
why: The client already understands how to request help; more instructions do not improve response timing.
Medication timing may be reviewed, but anticipated assistance directly addresses the demonstrated pattern.
A reminder does not resolve the gap between requesting help and receiving it.
Proactive toileting reduces urgent attempts while preserving the required walking assistance.
takeaway: Align assistance with predictable care needs.
learningObjective: Align assistance with predictable care needs.

title: Wheelchair transfer brakes
stem: A client is awaiting a planned transfer from bed into an empty wheelchair, but one wheelchair brake does not hold. A replacement wheelchair is available. What should the nurse arrange?
options: A transfer using a functioning chair and the approved method
A transfer with the intact brake fully engaged
A transfer with a second worker holding the faulty wheel
A transfer with the chair positioned firmly against the wall
why: A reliable transfer surface avoids loading defective equipment; the replacement should be introduced using an approved safe method.
One brake may allow the other side to move or rotate during loading.
Manual stabilization is not a dependable substitute for a functioning brake.
A wall may limit backward movement but does not reliably prevent rotation or side movement.
takeaway: Do not transfer from equipment with unreliable stabilization.
learningObjective: Do not transfer from equipment with unreliable stabilization.

title: Transfer reassessment
stem: A client normally uses a sit-to-stand device but cannot follow instructions today. What should guide transfer?
options: Yesterday's equipment plan
Current ability and an appropriate revised method
The client's usual body weight alone
The quickest available device
why: A previous plan may be unsafe after a functional change.
The device must match present participation and physical ability.
Weight is only one factor in safe device selection.
Availability does not establish suitability.
takeaway: Choose transfer equipment using current client function.
learningObjective: Choose transfer equipment using current client function.

title: Hoist sling tear
stem: A nurse finds a small tear in a sling before a dependent client's planned transfer. What is the best response?
options: Use the sling for a shorter transfer to the nearest chair
Select an intact sling of the same size from another lift
Remove the sling and obtain a compatible intact replacement
Leave the sling in place for reassessment at the next lift
why: The sling still bears the client's weight during a short transfer.
The same size does not establish compatibility with this lift or client.
Both material integrity and verified compatibility are required for safe loading.
Identified damaged equipment should be removed from service rather than left ready for reuse.
takeaway: Remove damaged lifting components from service.
learningObjective: Remove damaged lifting components from service.

title: Hoist preparation
stem: Before lifting a dependent client, which checks are necessary? Select all that apply.
options: Compatibility and condition of sling and lift
Required staff and client-specific plan
A sling chosen from its familiar colour and usual size label
Equipment capacity and attachment security
why: Compatibility and integrity are essential to safe loading.
Staffing and technique should match the assessed transfer.
A size label alone does not establish compatibility with the lift or client.
Capacity and secure attachment prevent mechanical failure.
takeaway: Check the full lifting system before loading it.
learningObjective: Check the full lifting system before loading it.

title: Client begins to collapse
stem: During assisted walking, a client's knees buckle. What should a trained nurse do?
options: Pull sharply upward by the arms
Try to keep the client standing alone
Step away to obtain a wheelchair
Use trained techniques to guide safely downward and call for help
why: Arm traction can injure the client and nurse.
Trying to hold full body weight may injure both people.
Leaving removes immediate support during the collapse.
A controlled descent reduces injury risk while assistance is obtained.
takeaway: Use trained fall-response techniques rather than lifting a collapsing client.
learningObjective: Use trained fall-response techniques rather than lifting a collapsing client.

title: Heavy repositioning
stem: Two nurses have adjusted the bed to working height, but repositioning a dependent client still requires excessive force. What is the best next response?
options: Obtain an approved repositioning aid and required assistance
Add one more worker to pull on the drawsheet
Lower the bed and repeat the manual manoeuvre
Change the drawsheet grip and repeat the manoeuvre
why: The load exceeds a safe manual approach; assessed equipment and staffing reduce force and friction.
Another worker alone may not adequately reduce friction or distribute the load safely.
A lower bed may worsen posture and does not reduce the client's load.
A different grip does not resolve the excessive force already identified.
takeaway: Escalate equipment needs when manual effort is unsafe.
learningObjective: Escalate equipment needs when manual effort is unsafe.

title: Slide-sheet use
stem: A worker proposes leaving a low-friction transfer sheet beneath a mobile client after repositioning. What should be checked?
options: Whether the sheet helped staff complete the transfer more quickly
Manufacturer instructions and sliding risk in this situation
Whether another client tolerated the sheet overnight
Whether the next shift usually removes it
why: Transfer efficiency does not establish safety for prolonged use under the client.
Some devices are not safe for continued use under an independently moving client.
Another client's experience does not establish safe use in this situation.
Custom does not establish device safety.
takeaway: Follow device instructions and reassess unintended sliding risk.
learningObjective: Follow device instructions and reassess unintended sliding risk.

title: Bed exit and rails
stem: A confused client has twice attempted to climb over fully raised bed rails despite reminders. Staff have assisted them back safely. Which plan best addresses the hazard now?
options: Keep full rails and move the bed nearer the desk
Keep full rails and increase alarm sensitivity
Review rail use and arrange a low bed with appropriate observation
Keep full rails and schedule more frequent orientation
why: Proximity supports response but retains the high climbing barrier.
An alarm detects movement but does not remove the climbing and entrapment hazard.
A reassessed less restrictive environment and observation address both climbing risk and the client's needs.
Orientation may help but has not prevented attempts and does not correct the equipment hazard.
takeaway: Bed rails can create hazards and require individualized assessment.
learningObjective: Bed rails can create hazards and require individualized assessment.

title: Restraint request
stem: A restless client repeatedly touches an intact dressing and says it feels uncomfortable. Family requests wrist restraints. The client is not causing immediate serious harm. What should the nurse do first?
options: Apply a protective cover over the dressing
Request a sedating PRN medication order
Seek authorization for temporary wrist restraints
Assess the discomfort and contributing causes
why: A cover may be useful after determining whether pain, irritation or another problem is present.
Sedation may mask a treatable cause and adds adverse-effect risks.
Restraint authorization does not replace assessing need and less restrictive measures.
The reported discomfort provides a potentially treatable explanation that should guide the response.
takeaway: Assess causes and alternatives before restrictive interventions.
learningObjective: Assess causes and alternatives before restrictive interventions.

title: Restrictive-device monitoring
stem: An authorized restraint is in use after alternatives failed. Which care remains necessary? Select all that apply.
options: Reassess ongoing need
Monitor circulation, skin and comfort
Wait until removal to offer toileting
Provide required observation and release care under policy
why: The intervention should not continue beyond its indication.
Restraints can impair circulation and damage tissue.
Elimination needs continue during restriction.
Monitoring and care mitigate foreseeable restraint harms.
takeaway: Authorization does not remove ongoing restraint assessment and care.
learningObjective: Authorization does not remove ongoing restraint assessment and care.

title: Restraint circulation change
stem: A restrained client's fingers become cool and pale. What is the priority?
options: Document at the next scheduled check
Relieve the restriction safely and assess urgently
Cover the hand and continue
Ask the client to move fingers more
why: A new circulation concern should not wait.
Possible impaired perfusion requires immediate correction and assessment.
Warming does not remove mechanical restriction.
Movement alone may not restore circulation.
takeaway: Respond immediately to possible restraint-related neurovascular compromise.
learningObjective: Respond immediately to possible restraint-related neurovascular compromise.

title: Elopement concern
stem: A disoriented resident has repeatedly passed an exit reminder and opened a door leading directly to traffic. The resident walks steadily but cannot explain how to return safely. Which immediate plan provides the most reliable protection?
options: Arrange additional family visits during the afternoon
Install a door alarm linked to the nursing station
Assign supervision while implementing safe exit controls
Move favourite activities farther from the exit
why: Family involvement may help but does not provide continuous accountable protection now.
An alarm alerts after movement begins and is an adjunct where traffic is immediately outside.
Assigned supervision protects now while an individualized environment plan addresses repeated unsafe exit access.
Meaningful activities can reduce exit-seeking but cannot alone assure protection from the immediate hazard.
takeaway: Match elopement precautions to the person's risk and environment.
learningObjective: Match elopement precautions to the person's risk and environment.

title: Missing vulnerable resident
stem: A cognitively impaired resident cannot be located during a planned check. What should happen?
options: Search alone before telling anyone
Wait for the next meal
Call family before activating the unit process
Activate the missing-person response and coordinate immediate search
why: A lone search can delay a coordinated response.
Waiting may allow the resident to reach hazards.
Family contact can accompany but should not delay the response.
Rapid coordination supports timely location and rescue.
takeaway: Act promptly when a vulnerable client is unexpectedly missing.
learningObjective: Act promptly when a vulnerable client is unexpectedly missing.

title: Seizure environment
stem: A client with recurrent seizures is resting in bed. Which preparation is appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep emergency equipment available according to plan
Remove nearby injury hazards
Keep a padded object ready to insert in the mouth
Ensure staff know the individualized response plan
why: Preparation supports timely airway and emergency response.
Clearing hazards reduces injury during involuntary movement.
Objects should not be forced into the mouth during a seizure.
A shared plan improves consistent response and escalation.
takeaway: Prepare the environment and team for the known seizure pattern.
learningObjective: Prepare the environment and team for the known seizure pattern.

title: Seizure during activity
stem: A client begins a generalized seizure while seated. What is the nurse's initial aim?
options: Restrain limb movements
Protect from injury and summon assistance
Give oral water
Obtain a full history before intervening
why: Forceful restraint can cause injury.
Immediate protection and help address current danger.
Oral intake during a seizure risks aspiration.
History follows immediate safety measures.
takeaway: During seizure activity, prioritize protection and assistance.
learningObjective: During seizure activity, prioritize protection and assistance.

title: Seizure timing
stem: During a witnessed seizure, which observation is especially important for subsequent decisions?
options: Whether the client recalls an aura after recovery
Whether the client missed a routine meal before the event
Onset and duration of seizure activity
Whether the client has a family history of seizures
why: Aura history can help but does not replace timing needed for immediate escalation.
Possible triggers matter, but seizure duration more directly guides urgent response.
Duration affects urgency and evaluation of the seizure pattern.
Family history does not characterize the urgency of this ongoing episode.
takeaway: Record seizure onset and duration accurately.
learningObjective: Record seizure onset and duration accurately.

title: Fire at bedside
stem: A small fire starts in bedding while a client is in immediate danger. A colleague is activating the alarm and calling for help. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Close the doors around the affected area
Locate the appropriate fire extinguisher
Disconnect nearby electrical equipment
Move the endangered client to safety
why: Containment matters but should not precede rescue of a client exposed to the burning bedding.
Extinguisher use follows safe rescue and the emergency plan when appropriate.
Removing a potential ignition source does not first remove the client from present danger.
The client is directly endangered and the alarm is already being activated, so immediate rescue is the priority.
takeaway: Protect people in immediate danger during a fire.
learningObjective: Protect people in immediate danger during a fire.

title: Smoke barrier
stem: A fire room has been evacuated and the alarm activated. The nurse reaches its open door while another team relocates clients in the adjoining corridor. What action most directly limits their smoke exposure?
options: Close the fire-room door under the emergency plan
Fetch an extinguisher from the next corridor
Collect care records for the receiving area
Move portable equipment into the safe area
why: Closing the door limits smoke spread while the coordinated evacuation continues.
Fire suppression may be needed but equipment retrieval does not contain the current smoke path.
Records support continuity but do not reduce immediate smoke exposure.
Equipment transfer does not first control smoke spreading from the open room.
takeaway: Use smoke containment and coordinated fire response.
learningObjective: Use smoke containment and coordinated fire response.

title: Evacuation accountability
stem: During evacuation, two relocated clients share a surname and one needs continuous oxygen. Which handoff document best supports safe receiving care?
options: The unit bed-assignment list printed before evacuation
A verified client roster with locations and support needs
The original census total with the number transferred
A medication summary sorted by the former room numbers
why: Previous beds may not match current locations and do not establish essential support.
Verified identities, destinations and current needs support both accountability and continuous oxygen delivery.
Counts cannot establish which particular client needs help or remains unaccounted for.
Medication information is useful but does not reliably establish current location and oxygen support.
takeaway: Track both identity and care needs during evacuation.
learningObjective: Track both identity and care needs during evacuation.

title: Extinguisher decision
stem: The alarm is active and clients have been evacuated. Smoke is increasing near a small fire. An untrained nurse has a clear exit, but fetching an extinguisher would require moving toward the smoke. What should the nurse do?
options: Approach with an extinguisher because the fire remains small
Wait near the fire for a colleague to demonstrate the equipment
Withdraw through the safe exit and report to trained responders
Retrieve the extinguisher and leave it beside the fire
why: Fire size does not establish that an untrained approach is safe.
Remaining near increasing smoke creates an exposure risk; real-time instruction does not replace training.
The clear exit permits safe withdrawal while the trained response is already activated.
Equipment retrieval would move this nurse toward smoke rather than protect the safe escape route.
takeaway: Use fire equipment only within training and a safe response plan.
learningObjective: Use fire equipment only within training and a safe response plan.

title: Ventilator battery contingency
stem: During a hospital power failure, a ventilator switches to battery operation and continues delivering the prescribed support. The client is stable. The nurse is trained in the unit contingency plan. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess the client and verify ongoing ventilator support
Use the illuminated battery icon to infer adequate remaining duration
Check battery capacity and the approved emergency-power connection
Move the plug to the nearest unlabelled outlet
Activate the contingency response and prepare the trained backup method
why: Clinical assessment and delivery checks confirm that support is actually continuing.
An icon establishes battery operation, not how long support can continue.
Verified capacity and an approved power route guide safe continuation before battery depletion.
An unlabelled outlet is not a verified emergency source.
Coordinated support and a ready backup protect the client if battery-supported ventilation fails.
takeaway: Verify actual support and remaining capacity when life-support equipment switches to backup power.
learningObjective: Evaluate battery-supported ventilation and prepare the trained contingency response.

title: Damaged electrical cord
stem: An infusion pump has exposed wiring in its power cord. An equivalent checked pump is available and the client requires uninterrupted therapy. What is safest?
options: Apply insulating tape to the exposed section
Replace the pump safely while maintaining the infusion
Complete this infusion using the pump's charged battery
Request repair after the current infusion finishes
why: Improvised insulation does not establish electrical safety.
A coordinated equipment change preserves therapy and removes the defective device from service.
Battery operation does not resolve the identified equipment defect when a safe replacement is available.
Continuing routine use postpones correction of a known hazard.
takeaway: Remove defective equipment while preserving essential therapy.
learningObjective: Remove defective equipment while preserving essential therapy.

title: Unexpected pump rate
stem: After a pump is moved, a stable client's saline infusion displays 125 mL/h. The handoff notes 75 mL/h, and a new order may have been entered. Which action should guide correction of the discrepancy?
options: Reprogram the pump to the rate remembered from handoff
Replace the pump with another unit at the displayed rate
Check the current order, pump settings and delivered volume
Ask the prescriber to rewrite the infusion prescription
why: The remembered rate may have been superseded; confirm the current prescription.
A new device at an unverified rate can reproduce the error.
Verification establishes the intended rate and possible exposure so treatment can be safely corrected.
A new prescription may not be needed if the current order resolves the discrepancy.
takeaway: Investigate a device setting discrepancy immediately.
learningObjective: Investigate a device setting discrepancy immediately.

title: Alarm fatigue pattern
stem: A monitored client is breathing comfortably with unchanged observations. The oxygen-saturation trace disappears when a visibly loose finger sensor moves, then returns when it is held correctly. What should the nurse do next?
options: Reduce the alarm volume to the night setting
Lower the saturation threshold for this client
Request a different monitor for the bedside
Secure or replace the sensor and verify the signal
why: Volume adjustment does not resolve the lost signal or preserve reliable detection.
Changing a clinical threshold does not correct a contact problem.
The movement-related contact failure should be corrected before attributing it to the whole monitor.
The observed contact problem explains the artifact; correcting it and confirming readings restores monitoring.
takeaway: Resolve nuisance-alarm causes without removing needed safeguards.
learningObjective: Resolve nuisance-alarm causes without removing needed safeguards.

title: Transport oxygen supply
stem: A client needs oxygen during a longer-than-usual transfer. What must be verified?
options: Adequate supply and functioning delivery for the expected trip plus contingency
That the cylinder was replaced at the start of the shift
That oxygen flows when the valve is opened briefly
That the previous client used the cylinder briefly
why: Trip planning must account for consumption and possible delay.
Earlier replacement does not establish enough remaining supply for this trip.
A brief flow check does not establish duration or contingency capacity.
Previous use does not quantify what remains.
takeaway: Check transport support capacity before leaving the care area.
learningObjective: Check transport support capacity before leaving the care area.

title: Tubing misconnections
stem: Several tubes lie together beneath bedding before reconnection after transfer. What is the safest approach?
options: Match tubing by approximate diameter
Trace each line from client to source before connecting
Use the closest available connector
Ask which line was disconnected last
why: Similar diameters do not establish function.
Tracing confirms the intended route and prevents misconnections.
Physical fit alone does not guarantee the correct route.
Sequence memory does not verify line identity.
takeaway: Trace lines fully before connecting them.
learningObjective: Trace lines fully before connecting them.

title: MRI screening gap
stem: A client arrives for MRI and mentions an implanted device not documented on the screening form. What next?
options: Proceed if no device symptoms exist
Ask the client to remove jewellery only
Pause and notify MRI staff for device-specific verification
Use the previous CT screening results
why: Absence of symptoms does not establish MRI compatibility.
Jewellery removal does not address an implanted device.
MRI staff must verify the specific device and conditions.
CT screening does not assess magnetic-field hazards.
takeaway: Resolve implant uncertainty before MRI exposure.
learningObjective: Resolve implant uncertainty before MRI exposure.

title: Equipment recall
stem: A manufacturer notice directs removal of pumps with serial numbers 4100–4199 because the startup test may miss a fault. A nurse is assigned to implement the notice. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Match unit serial numbers against the affected range
Clear an affected pump after a successful startup test
Arrange checked replacement pumps for affected infusions
Return unaffected pumps of the same model for testing
Record the affected device identifiers and actions taken
why: The defined range identifies which devices require the recall response.
The notice specifically states that the startup test may not detect this fault.
Replacement planning avoids creating an interruption while affected devices are removed.
The stated notice does not require withdrawing unaffected devices.
Documented identification and action support traceability and completion of the response.
takeaway: Manage recalls through device identification and safe continuity.
learningObjective: Manage recalls through device identification and safe continuity.

title: Wrong-client screen
stem: A nurse opens a chart to administer treatment but the displayed birth date differs from the wristband. What next?
options: Trust the room assignment
Resolve the identity mismatch before proceeding
Use the first name alone
Ask the client if they recognize the treatment
why: Room assignment is not a reliable identifier.
A mismatch must be clarified before care is linked to a record.
First names may be shared.
Treatment familiarity cannot establish identity.
takeaway: Stop when clinical identifiers conflict.
learningObjective: Stop when clinical identifiers conflict.

title: Specimen label mismatch
stem: A collected specimen label does not match the client's verified identifiers. The collector has left the bedside. What should the nurse do?
options: Replace the label using the chart currently open
Confirm the intended client with the collector by telephone
Contact the laboratory for the approved correction or recollection process
Send the specimen with a note describing the discrepancy
why: An open chart does not establish the identity of the specimen in the tube.
The collector may contribute information, but a recollection or correction decision must preserve the approved identification process.
The laboratory process determines whether identity can be securely corrected or the sample must be recollected.
Processing an unresolved identity discrepancy risks misdirected results and treatment.
takeaway: Resolve specimen identity errors before laboratory processing.
learningObjective: Resolve specimen identity errors before laboratory processing.

title: Surgical-site discrepancy
stem: Before an elective procedure, the consent and site marking name different sides. What is the best action?
options: Use the visible site mark to guide preparation
Use the side recorded on the operating schedule
Confirm the side with the awake client and amend the mark
Pause until the procedural team reconciles the intended site
why: The mark itself may be the incorrect element.
Scheduling information can also contain an error.
Client confirmation is important evidence, but the team must reconcile consent, records and marking before progression.
A coordinated pause resolves conflicting evidence and prevents wrong-site treatment.
takeaway: Resolve procedure and site discrepancies before starting.
learningObjective: Resolve procedure and site discrepancies before starting.

title: Allergy wristband conflict
stem: A client with a confirmed latex allergy is prepared for a scheduled procedure, but latex supplies are on the tray. What should the nurse arrange before proceeding?
options: Replace the latex-containing supplies with suitable alternatives
Cover exposed latex components with a sterile drape
Administer the prescribed antihistamine before using the tray
Increase allergy observations during the procedure
why: Avoiding the known allergen addresses the preventable exposure.
A cover does not reliably eliminate exposure from latex-containing equipment.
Premedication does not make known allergen exposure safe.
Observation may detect a reaction but does not prevent the avoidable exposure.
takeaway: Reconcile allergy information with actual equipment and supplies.
learningObjective: Reconcile allergy information with actual equipment and supplies.

title: Hazardous spill
stem: An unidentified chemical spills beside a treatment area. What is the safest initial approach?
options: Absorb the spill with standard disposable towels
Restrict access and activate the spill response
Dilute the spill with a container of water
Move the nearby treatment supplies to another shelf
why: Absorption methods and protection depend on the chemical hazard.
Access control prevents additional exposure while trained staff identify and manage the spill.
Water can be incompatible with some chemicals.
Protecting supplies does not first protect people from the unidentified spill.
takeaway: Identify and contain chemical hazards through the approved response.
learningObjective: Identify and contain chemical hazards through the approved response.

title: Safety data sheet
stem: A nurse checks the supplied safety summary before using an unfamiliar disinfectant. Which preparations follow these instructions? Select all that apply.
options: Use the specified chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection
Add water to reduce the vapour from this ready-to-use product
Work in the designated ventilated cleaning area
Combine it with the usual bleach solution for stronger cleaning
Locate the eyewash and the product exposure instructions
why: The summary specifies hand and eye protection for splash and contact hazards.
The supplied instructions identify the product as ready to use; an improvised dilution changes its intended preparation.
The designated ventilated area follows the stated inhalation precaution.
The summary explicitly prohibits mixing with bleach.
A known eyewash location and accessible instructions support prompt exposure response.
takeaway: Use safety information before handling unfamiliar hazardous products.
exhibit: Ready to use; do not dilute
Specified chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection
Begin eyewash promptly; obtain medical assistance
learningObjective: Use safety information before handling unfamiliar hazardous products.

title: Chemical eye exposure
stem: A cleaning agent splashes into a worker's eye. A colleague is obtaining the product information and calling for assistance. What should begin immediately?
options: Telephone occupational health for an appointment
Retrieve the product safety data sheet
Begin irrigation at the emergency eyewash
Remove the worker's contaminated outer clothing
why: Calling for assistance is already underway and should not delay eye decontamination.
A colleague is obtaining this information while exposure must be stopped.
Prompt irrigation reduces ongoing eye exposure while product-specific guidance is obtained.
Clothing decontamination may be required, but it does not first remove the chemical from the affected eye.
takeaway: Begin prompt eye irrigation after chemical exposure.
learningObjective: Begin prompt eye irrigation after chemical exposure.

title: Compressed cylinder transport
stem: A transport oxygen cylinder does not fit securely in the stretcher's installed holder. Which arrangement should be used for the transfer?
options: Place it in the stretcher's equipment basket
Have the escort carry it beside the stretcher
Use a similar holder designed for a smaller cylinder
Use an approved carrier that secures this cylinder
why: A general basket may not restrain a cylinder against movement or impact.
Hand carrying does not provide the designed restraint for transport.
A superficially similar holder does not establish a secure compatible fit.
The carrier must be compatible and secure the cylinder during movement.
takeaway: Secure compressed gas cylinders using designed transport equipment.
learningObjective: Secure compressed gas cylinders using designed transport equipment.

title: Hot-water testing
stem: A client with reduced sensation requires bathing. Unit policy requires checking water with a bath thermometer before contact. Which check should guide water safety?
options: Measure the water using the bath thermometer
Ask the client whether a hand in the water feels comfortable
Test the water briefly using the nurse's hand
Confirm that the tap remains at its preset position
why: The required objective check protects a client whose temperature perception is unreliable.
Reduced sensation limits the usefulness of the client's subjective response.
A brief hand test is subjective and does not meet the stated measuring method.
The tap setting does not confirm the temperature actually delivered.
takeaway: Use reliable temperature checks when sensation is impaired.
learningObjective: Use reliable temperature checks when sensation is impaired.

title: Heating-device risk
stem: A client with longstanding neuropathy describes an uncomfortable cold feeling in a numb foot. Skin is intact, colour and pulses are unchanged, and the foot is warm to touch. Which comfort measure is safest while the symptom plan is reviewed?
options: Apply a heating pad on its lowest setting
Use a loose dry sock and reassess comfort
Wrap a hot-water bottle in a towel beside the foot
Prepare a warm foot soak for the client
why: A low setting can still burn insensate skin before discomfort is recognized.
A nonthermal insulating measure avoids exposing numb tissue to an uncontrolled heat source.
Wrapping does not reliably prevent prolonged heat injury in insensate tissue.
Reduced sensation makes excessive water heat harder to detect.
takeaway: Reduced sensation increases risk from therapeutic heat.
learningObjective: Reduced sensation increases risk from therapeutic heat.

title: Hospital-acquired injury review
stem: Adhesive removal leaves a visible skin flap on a frail client's forearm. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Assess the flap, bleeding, pain and surrounding skin
Add adhesive allergy to the client's alert record
Protect the wound according to the assessed wound-care plan
Use the same adhesive to anchor routine dry gauze
Review adhesive choice and removal technique before the next dressing
why: The visible tissue disruption needs a focused assessment to guide care.
A skin tear after removal may reflect mechanical trauma; it does not by itself establish an allergy.
The wound should be protected using care matched to its assessed condition.
Repeating a traumatic adhesive approach may cause further damage; dressing and securement should be reassessed.
Changing a contributing product or technique can reduce recurrence.
takeaway: Use injury findings to improve the next care episode.
learningObjective: Use injury findings to improve the next care episode.

title: Bed entrapment gap
stem: A replacement mattress creates a large gap beside the bed rail for a frail client. The manufacturer confirms this mattress is incompatible and no approved gap insert exists. Which is the best ongoing solution?
options: Fill the gap with firm pillows beneath the sheet
Request a custom foam insert from maintenance
Replace the setup with compatible approved equipment
Lower the rail and schedule closer observation
why: Pillows can shift and are not a validated entrapment correction.
An improvised insert does not establish a tested safe configuration.
Approved compatible components correct the known equipment mismatch.
Closer observation may support temporary safety arrangements but does not correct the unsuitable equipment for ongoing use.
takeaway: Assess compatibility when bed components change.
learningObjective: Assess compatibility when bed components change.

title: Accessible call system
stem: A client cannot press a standard call button because of severe hand weakness. Speech is faint, but the client reliably moves one knee against a switch during assessment. Which adjustment best supports independent calls for help?
options: Arrange a voice-activated call device
Move the standard button onto the client's lap
Schedule additional staff rounding visits
Provide a suitable knee-activated call switch
