stem: A client listed as independently mobile now requires a mechanical lift. The evacuation plan still lists independent walking. What should happen?
options: Keep the original designation until the annual drill
Ask the client to practise walking during an alarm
Update the plan with current assistance and equipment needs
Remove the client from the evacuation list until reviewed
why: An outdated plan may fail during a real emergency.
An alarm is not the time to test unsafe mobility.
Current needs must determine planned evacuation support.
Omission would make accountability and rescue less reliable.
takeaway: Update emergency plans when functional assistance needs change.
learningObjective: Update emergency plans when functional assistance needs change.

title: Latex exposure from visitors
stem: A client with a severe latex allergy receives latex balloons from visitors. The nurse has already selected nonlatex care supplies. What next?
options: Allow balloons because they are not medical supplies
Keep them near the window rather than the bed
Ask the client to report symptoms before removal
Remove the exposure and explain suitable alternatives
why: Environmental latex sources can still create exposure.
Room placement does not reliably eliminate the risk.
Waiting permits avoidable allergen contact.
The prevention plan should include nonclinical items brought into the room.
takeaway: Include visitor items when managing environmental allergens.
learningObjective: Include visitor items when managing environmental allergens.

title: Shared personal grooming tool
stem: Two long-term-care residents share an electric razor, and one has small shaving cuts. What is best?
options: Provide individual equipment or validated processing according to policy
Rinse the razor quickly between residents
Share only when both have the same room
Remove visible hair and assume the blades are safe
why: Potential blood contamination requires an appropriate individual-use or processing plan.
Quick rinsing may not decontaminate internal cutting surfaces.
Room sharing does not make blood exposure safe.
Visible hair removal does not establish disinfection.
takeaway: Consider blood contamination when sharing personal-care equipment.
learningObjective: Consider blood contamination when sharing personal-care equipment.

title: Clean uniform after splash
stem: A nurse's uniform becomes visibly contaminated with body fluid during care. What should happen?
options: Cover the wet area with a clean gown for the rest of the shift
Change contaminated clothing through the approved process and clean exposed skin
Wait until the uniform is dry before visiting the next client
Apply hand rub directly to the fabric and continue
why: Covering does not remove contamination already present.
Clothing and exposed skin should be addressed to limit further contact.
Drying does not establish decontamination.
Hand rub is not an approved clothing-cleaning method.
takeaway: Remove contaminated clothing from ongoing clinical contact.
learningObjective: Remove contaminated clothing from ongoing clinical contact.

title: Infection precautions and mobility
stem: A stable client on contact precautions needs daily walking to prevent deconditioning. Which planning actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Coordinate a route and timing consistent with local precautions
Cancel all mobility solely because contact precautions are present
Contain drainage and perform appropriate hand hygiene before movement
Communicate equipment cleaning needs to involved staff
why: Planned movement can support care goals while limiting exposure.
Precautions do not automatically justify avoidable immobility.
Source containment and hand hygiene reduce environmental spread.
Staff need a shared plan for equipment processing.
takeaway: Plan essential activity within the required transmission precautions.
learningObjective: Plan essential activity within the required transmission precautions.

title: Reusable equipment without instructions
stem: A donated reusable device has no available manufacturer processing instructions. What is best before clinical use?
options: Use the strongest disinfectant available
Copy instructions from a similar-looking device
Obtain validated processing and use information or choose an approved alternative
Rely on intact packaging from the donor
why: Stronger chemicals may damage the device without ensuring appropriate processing.
Similar appearance does not establish compatible materials or methods.
Safe reuse requires a validated process for the actual device.
Donor packaging does not establish clinical readiness.
takeaway: Do not improvise reprocessing for an unfamiliar reusable device.
learningObjective: Do not improvise reprocessing for an unfamiliar reusable device.

title: Processing a critical instrument
stem: Reusable forceps will enter normally sterile tissue during a planned procedure. A colleague proposes high-level disinfection to shorten turnaround. What should guide preparation?
options: Use high-level disinfection if no visible blood remains
Use a surface disinfectant and then rinse with sterile water
Place cleaned forceps in a sterile wrapper without further processing
Use a validated sterilization process appropriate for the instrument
why: Critical instruments entering sterile tissue require sterilization, not just high-level disinfection.
Surface disinfection and rinsing do not establish sterility.
Sterile packaging does not sterilize the instrument placed inside.
The processing level must match entry into normally sterile tissue.
takeaway: Critical instruments require appropriate sterilization before use.
learningObjective: Critical instruments require appropriate sterilization before use.

title: Infection-risk discharge equipment
stem: A client leaves with reusable home-care equipment but cannot describe how to clean it. What should the nurse arrange?
options: A demonstration using the device instructions and a return demonstration
A general leaflet on hospital infection rates
Advice to use whichever household cleaner is strongest
A plan to replace the device whenever it looks dirty
why: Device-specific practice verifies a safe reproducible method.
General statistics do not teach the required technique.
Unapproved chemicals may damage equipment or fail to disinfect.
Visual dirt alone is not a reliable processing schedule.
takeaway: Verify the client's ability to perform device-specific home cleaning.
learningObjective: Verify the client's ability to perform device-specific home cleaning.

title: Safety evaluation after equipment change
stem: A unit replaces a transfer device with a newer model. What evidence best supports safe implementation?
options: The delivery invoice confirms the model arrived
Staff demonstrate the new procedure and clients are reassessed for suitability
The new device resembles the old one
The first shift reports completing transfers more quickly
why: Receipt does not establish competent clinical use.
Observed competence and client fit test the relevant safety requirements.
Similarity does not guarantee identical technique or limitations.
Efficiency alone does not establish safe use.
takeaway: Evaluate competence and client suitability after equipment changes.
learningObjective: Evaluate competence and client suitability after equipment changes.

title: Inadequate sterilization cycle
stem: A reprocessing alert states that a load did not reach the required sterilization cycle parameters. Several unopened packs from that load are on the unit. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Withhold the affected packs from clinical use
Identify and manage affected items through the recall/reprocessing pathway
Use the packs if their external wrapping remains intact
Notify the relevant team and follow the approved corrective process
why: Inadequate processing means sterility cannot be relied upon.
Load tracing permits appropriate containment and reprocessing.
Intact wrapping cannot compensate for a failed sterilization process.
Coordinated correction prevents exposure and addresses the processing failure.
takeaway: Packaging integrity does not compensate for inadequate sterilization.
learningObjective: Packaging integrity does not compensate for inadequate sterilization.
